newsitem.title: USA: Texan vies for hop honors, but he may be longshot.
newsitem.headline: Texan vies for hop honors, but he may be longshot.

text.p: It may be a long shot, but bottles of Texas-style smoked beer tasting like "liquid ribs" and other creative homebrews could soon be on store shelves.

Carlos Kelley, 40, had never brewed more than 10 gallons of his dark-coloured concoction before he and eight other finalists in the second annual World Homebrew Contest travelled to the Boston Beer Co. brewery in Boston.
Three winners will receive $5,000 cash, an expense paid trip to any beer capital of the world and have their beer bottled and sold on store shelves across the country under the brand name LongShot.
Lovers of "lawnmower beer" may not care for his smoked beer, Kelley said, but Boston Beer has carved out a profitable niche of the "specialty" beer market with its premium-priced brews.

"When you drink this beer, you can almost chew the smoked meat," said the Fort Worth, Texas native, dressed in a black cowboy hat and white overalls with 'finalist' stitched in red over his right breast.
Beverley Graham, 53, hated the taste of beer until her husband got a homebrew kit for Christmas last year and created a hoppy "California Common" beer he thought she would like.
Now finalists in the contest, the Grahams may have their beer sold nationally with their signatures on every bottle.

"I guess there is a beer out there for me," said Graham, who lives in the Chicago suburb of Park Ridge. "I like wine but we got this beer-making kit for Christmas from our kids so we started brewing in January."

Illegal until 1978, homebrewing has exploded in popularity and changed the habits of beer drinkers everywhere. The American Homebrewers Association, which has 25,000 members, estimates one million-to-1.5 million Americans make their own beer.

"Interconnecting the leading speciality brewer and the homebrewing movement is a rather shrewd marketing move," said Benjamin Steinman, editor of the biweekly Beer Marketer's Insight. "That's especially true since not all elements of the homebrewing movement are fond of the Boston Beer Company."

Boston Beer founder James Koch made his first batch of Samuel Adams in his mother's kitchen in 1984. Since then, the company has grown larger than the next six largest speciality brewers combined and spurred the major brewers to create thier own "craft brews".
However, some homebrewers have charged that Boston Beer has strayed from its homebrewing roots by contracting out with other brewers to make its beers.
Boston Beer Co. began selling the first three winners of its LongShot contest -- a hazlenut brown ale, a black lager and an American pale ale -- in May to apparent success.
Steinman said he believed LongShot was selling well for a new brand and he had heard Boston Beer expected to sell 45,000 barrels from its May introduction to the end of the year.
Rob Cushman, director of new brand development at Boston Beer, said sales have met expectations in most markets but the long-term trend is difficult to forecast.

Kelley's brew, which he calls "On Top With Ol' Smokey", Graham's "California Common" and the other seven finalists will be judged on Nov. 1, when Boston Beer will name three winners. The three new LongShot beers will be sold nationally in February or March, Cushman said.
Kelley, who tasted his first smoked beer while studying languages in Germany in the late 1970s, said winning the contest would be only an added bonus.
"I've already won," Kelley said. "To have somebody fly me up to Boston and stay at a $100 hotel. I'm the guy who stays at the Motel 6 when I go anywhere."
